summary: This standards-track RFC specifies the data model and structure of a framework for provisioning Session Establishment Data into Session Data Registries and SIP service provider data stores. It is called the Session Peering Provisioning Framework.

eli5.summary: A shared form for entering the information that tells phone networks how to connect calls to each other.

questions: how does sip peering provisioning work
subtitle: A data model for telling a shared registry how phone and SIP networks should route sessions to each other.

tldr.problem: Service providers use routing registries to decide where to send VoIP, SMS and MMS sessions, but they need a common way to load their routing data into those registries and share it with chosen peers.
tldr.mechanism: SPPF defines the objects (Public Identifiers, Destination Groups, SED Groups, SED Records, offers and Egress Routes), the operations on them, and the requirements for the protocol that carries them, while leaving the wire protocol to a separate document.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard. A server must support the SOAP binding in RFC 7878, and the framework itself stays neutral about the substrate.

today: RFC 7877 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its SOAP binding is RFC 7878.

sections.title: Why a Provisioning Framework
sections.content:
Service providers and enterprises use routing databases called Registries to make session routing decisions for Voice over IP, SMS and Multimedia Messaging Service traffic. RFC 7877 is narrowly focused on how data gets into those Registries. The use cases behind it are in RFC 6461.

That earlier document describes three provisioning flows: client to Registry, Registry to local data repository, and Registry to Registry. SPPF covers only the first: a client provisioning Session Establishment Data (SED) into a Registry. SED is the set of parameters that outgoing border elements need to start a session, and it is typically used by SIP-signaling systems to route a call to the next hop for the called domain.

The framework must support two deployment scenarios: a resolution system that returns a Lookup Function (identifying the target domain), and one that returns a Location Routing Function (the address of the Signaling Function in the target domain).
sections.eli5: Phone companies need a shared place to write down how to reach each other. SPPF is the rulebook for how a company writes its entries into that shared place.

sections.title: Roles and Terminology
sections.content:
A Client initiates a provisioning request and a Server receives it. These roles apply only to the connection, so a Registry can also act as a client when it opens a connection, for example to distribute data to a provider.

The Registry operates a master database of SED for one or more Registrants. A Registrant is the holder of the SED being provisioned and is identified by the rant element. A Registrar performs provisioning operations on behalf of a Registrant; in other words, the Registrar is the SPPF client. The roles are logically separate so one Registrar may serve more than one Registrant, but it need not. A Peering Organization is an entity to which a Registrant's SED Groups are made visible.
sections.eli5: The registry is the big phone book, the registrant owns an entry, and the registrar is the clerk who writes it down for them. Peers are the companies allowed to read it.

sections.title: The Data Model
sections.content:
SPPF is built from a small set of linked objects. All first-class objects extend BasicObjType, which carries the Registrant (rant), the Registrar (rar), and creation and modification dates (cDate, mDate). The Registry stores the dates and MUST ignore any date values the client sends.

  • Public Identifier: the key used for lookups. It can be a telephone number (TN), a TN range, a TN prefix, a PSTN routing number (RN) or a URI.
  • Destination Group: a named group of Public Identifiers that share common SED.
  • SED Record: the data a resolution system returns for a successful query. The concrete types are URIType, NAPTRType and NSType.
  • SED Group: ties together Destination Groups, SED Records and the peering organizations allowed to see the result.
  • Egress Route: lets an originating provider pick a specific egress border element for a target's ingress route.
  • Organization: an entity that can be a Registrant, a Registrar and a peering organization.

This indirection is the point of the design. A change to one SED Group or SED Record replaces what would otherwise be millions of updates to individual Public Identifier records.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing the same directions on every phone number, you put numbers into folders and attach one set of directions to the folder. Change the directions once and every number in the folder is updated.

sections.title: Public Identifiers, SED Groups and Offers
sections.content:
A TN, an RN, a TN range (TNRType, a start and end TN), a TN prefix (TNPType) and a URI each have their own type. A TN can carry corInfo, which lets the Registrant claim to be the carrier-of-record. The Registry sets the outcome fields cor and corDate. What happens when a claim disagrees with the Registry's authority data is a matter of policy and beyond the scope of the document.

A Public Identifier in a Destination Group gets its SED through the SED Groups linked to that group. One not in any Destination Group uses the SED Records attached directly to it. A SED Group has isInSvc to say whether it is in service, a priority, and sourceIdent entries for source-based routing. Each sourceIdent pairs a scheme (uri, ip or rootDomain) with a regular expression, and the group's SED is only returned if a criterion matches the resolution request.

Access is controlled by a SED Group Offer. The Registrant offers a SED Group; the recipient can accept or reject it. Only after an offer is accepted is the recipient added to the group's peeringOrg list, which cannot be set directly. The offer's status is controlled by the server: offered when added, accepted once accepted. A rejected offer is deleted, even if it was previously accepted.
sections.eli5: A company can send another company a note saying it may use its directions. Only after the other company says yes does it get added to the list of people who can use them.

sections.title: Framework Operations
sections.content:
The framework defines the operations a conforming substrate protocol MUST provide: Add, Delete, Get, Accept, Reject and Get Server Details. Operations that may change persistent objects SHOULD include a transaction ID, and any operation MAY name a minor version.

Add creates the object if its key does not exist, and otherwise replaces its properties, so Add also modifies. Delete must also remove cross-references: deleting a SED Group removes its links to Destination Groups and SED Records and deletes its SED Group Offers. Deletes MUST be atomic. Get is meant to aid provisioning (logging, auditing, dependency checks) and is not a replacement for resolution protocols such as ENUM and SIP. Accept and Reject act on SED Group Offers. Get Server Details returns the server's status and supported major and minor versions.
sections.eli5: You can add an entry, remove it, look at it, say yes or no to an offer, or ask the clerk what version of the rules they follow. Removing something also cleans up everything that pointed to it.

sections.title: Requirements on the Substrate Protocol
sections.content:
SPPF does not define how its messages travel. It states what the carrying protocol must provide. None of the transports directly over IP meet the requirements, so one choice is provided in RFC 7878 (SOAP), and an SPPF server MUST support it.

The substrate must be connection oriented and use a request and response model, with a response for every request so a client can tell success from failure. It SHOULD support both short-lived and long-lived connections and datasets of various sizes, MUST allow responses to be correlated with requests, and MUST support near real-time responses. It MUST let the server authenticate the client, and it MUST provide data integrity protection.

Section 5.3 lists the response types every server MUST implement, including request succeeded, request syntax invalid, request too large, version not supported, command invalid, object does not exist and attribute value invalid. The last two MUST NOT be used interchangeably: a malformed object key gets the attribute error, while a well-formed key that matches nothing gets the not-exist error.
sections.eli5: The rulebook says the delivery method must be able to prove who is sending, keep the message from being tampered with, and always send an answer back.

sections.title: XML Encoding, Extensibility and IANA
sections.content:
XML is the encoding format. Time values use xs:dateTime and MUST be in UTC, written like 2010-05-30T09:30:10Z; a value with a time-zone offset is not acceptable. Organization IDs follow the form namespace:value, for example iana-en:32473. Names used in object keys are compared case-insensitively using toCasefold().

Instances SHOULD begin with an XML declaration. UTF-8 is the RECOMMENDED encoding, and clients and servers MUST accept a UTF-8 byte order mark though emitting one is NOT RECOMMENDED. The ext elements are the extension points. Extensions used beyond private installations need to be documented in an RFC, and the first one is expected to define an IANA registry of extensions. A protocol may use another data format such as JSON, as long as it meets the requirements of the XSD.

Two URNs are registered: the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:sppf:base:1 and the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:sppf:1. IANA also created a registry titled "SPPF OrgIdType Namespaces". The initial entry is iana-en, for IANA Enterprise Numbers. Future entries use the "RFC Required" policy.
sections.eli5: Everything is written in a tidy, tag-based text format with one agreed way to write times and company names, so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations handle data that is confidential and critical, for multiple Registrars and Registrants, so they must address confidentiality, authentication and authorization. Authorization rules (which Registrars may create, change, delete or view each object type for a given Registrant) are a matter of policy, but every implementation must specify them.

Denial of service is the main concern. SPPF relies on the substrate for authentication, so servers SHOULD be ready for authentication floods. Batch requests are stopped and rolled back on failure, which a hostile client could abuse by repeatedly sending large failing batches. The suggested response is to watch for excessive rollbacks and limit XML message and batch size.

The text also covers information disclosure through logs (SPPF implementations MAY support object-level encryption), optional non-repudiation, replay attacks (the optional client transaction identifier helps detect replayed responses), and a compromised or malicious intermediary such as a Registrar, since data may be in clear text before or after it crosses a protected connection.
sections.eli5: Since this data decides where phone calls go, only the right people may change it. The rules also warn about people flooding the system with junk and about a go-between peeking at the data.
